Title: Enhanced oily wastewater treatment: silver nanoparticles-coated graphene oxide/MXene nanocomposite membranes

Enhanced oily wastewater treatment: silver nanoparticles‑coated 
graphene oxide/MXene nanocomposite membranes
Zaina Algarni1 · Aseel Salah Mansoor2 · Usama Kadem Radi3 · Abdelfattah Amari4 · Naim Ben Ali5 ·

Abstract
There's growing interest in using membrane technology to treat oily wastewater in industries. Nevertheless, membrane foul-
ing is still a major challenge for removing oil particles from the wastewater. As reducing the membrane fouling requires 
material and surface science insights, in this work, a nanocomposite membrane was investigated for oily wastewater treat-
ment using synthesized silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) coated graphene oxide (GO)/MXene nanocomposite. The synthesized 
nanocomposite underwent characterization through FT-IR, XRD, FE-SEM, EDX, and Raman spectroscopy; and in order to 
characterize the fabricated membranes, SEM, and AFM analysis were applied and the membrane properties such as Hard-
ness, Young’s modulus, thickness, swelling ratio, and Water Contact Angle were studied. The efficiency of the produced 
membranes was assessed by computing the membrane's oil rejection and permeate flow; the results showed that the rejec-
tion was upper than 99.0% and the permeate flux was obtained as high as 160 L/m2 h. The study of the membrane surface 
charge by zeta potential analysis showed that the membrane performance could be optimized in terms of antibacterial and 
anti-fouling using synthesized nanocomposite membranes; that fully align with the findings of the efficiency of killing the 
bacteria (EKB) of different membranes using S. aureus as a Gram-positive and E. coli as a Gram-negative bacterium. The 
results of membrane fouling analysis showed that the modified membranes with FRR of 96.9% have higher sustainability 
compared to the PA6 neat membrane (FRR = 65.6%). Moreover, the classic Hermia fouling model revealed that the fouling 
mechanism of intermediate blocking best explains how fouling affects the membrane's performance.
Keywords  Oily wastewater treatment · Membrane-based process · Anti-fouling membrane · Silver nanoparticles · MXene

Introduction
Composites are one of the most important materials in 
today's modern world. The composites are composed of 
at least two components, a continuous matrix phase and 
a dispersed phase material; which are generally divided 
into three categories: Macro-Composites, Micro-Com-
posites and Nano-Composites (Wolff 2004). Because of 
the high surface-to-volume ratio of nanocomposites, there 
is a strong affinity between the matrix and the dispersed 
phase, which caused unique mechanical, chemical, electri-
cal, optical, and catalytic properties (Hamta et al. 2018).
Messaoudi et al. (2022) investigated Eriobotrya japon-
ica leaves/MgO nanocomposite for water purification. In 
this work, the hydrothermal method has been applied as 
an environmentally friendly method for the preparation of 
nanocomposite absorbent. They have claimed that accord-
ing to the investigations, the prepared nanocomposite has 
been very useful for removing tartrazine from water.
In 2022, Wu et al. (2022) presented a single-step approach 
for the production of hard porous nanocomposites, using 
biochar nanoparticles and polyacrylamide hydrogel matrix. 
The results show that polyacrylamide matrix gives high 
mechanical strength to the structure and biochar provides 
high adsorption capacity in removing water pollutants.
Nanocomposites can also be used to prepare conduc-
tive polymers for water purification and energy storage. 
Conductive polymers are organic macromolecules that 
introduce both the properties of metals and polymers 
into the system. Recently, the synthesis method of metal 
oxide placed on polyaniline for use in photocatalysts and 
supercapacitors has been studied. The performance of this 
material in terms of photocatalysis and electrochemical 
has made it a suitable and low-cost method for energy 
storage and water purification (Shahabuddin et al. 2022).
Behnamian et al. (2022) studied ­CuAl2O4–Ag nanocom-
posite as a photocatalyst in the water treatment industry in 
2022. In this work, copper–silver aluminate nanocompos-
ite has been fabricated by sol–gel method with the help of 
organic acid. The synthesized material has been investi-
gated for the removal of methylene blue.
Roy et al. (2022) created a nanocomposite consisting of 
graphene oxide (GO), keratin, and chitosan to serve as an 
adsorbent for eliminating turbidity in wastewater. In this 
article, nanocomposite is prepared by placing keratin and 
chitosan on the GO surface. It was reported that in addi-
tion to reducing water turbidity, the BOD, COD, TSS and 
TDS of water can be reduced. This nanocomposite also 
shows some magnetic property due to the small magnetic 
property of GO (Roy et al. 2022).
Understanding the influence of environmental factors, 
such as temperature, on system performance remains 
crucial. Studies on hydraulic valve systems, like those 
conducted by Hong et al. (2023), have highlighted the 
importance of temperature control in ensuring optimal 
operation. Similar considerations may be relevant to our 
membrane-based wastewater treatment process. In recent 
years, magnetic iron-based Metal–Organic Framework 
(MOF) has been investigated to remove dyes from waste-
water of textile industries. For example, Mousavi et al. 
(2022) succeeded in purifying water by photocatalytic 
method by synthesizing α-Fe2O3@C@SiO2/TiO2 nano-
composite. This method consists of two dry steps without 
using traditional reagents.
According to the type of matrix, there are three categories 
of nanocomposite; the first category is nanocomposite with 
ceramic matrix, the second category is nanocomposite with 
metal matrix, and the third one is the nanocomposite with 
polymer matrix. One of the polymer-based nanocomposites 
is the nanocomposite membrane which can be applied for 
oily wastewater treatment because of their high capacity, 
high efficiency, and better removal of contaminants (Hamta 
and Dehghani 2017).
Boron nitride/silver/GO has also been used as a nanocom-
posite to improve the antibacterial properties of polyether 
sulfone membranes in water purification (Vatanpour et al. 
2022). In this way, the prepared nanocomposite has created 
a membrane with high permeability, antibacterial, separation 
capability and high mechanical resistance. The findings of 
Zhang et al. (2023) on servo valves underscore the critical 
role of structural design in influencing fluid flow behavior. 
By applying these principles to our nanocomposite mem-
branes, we aim to optimize pore structure and fluid dynamics 
for improved performance.
One of the choices for the upcoming era of high-perfor-
mance membranes is nanocomposite membranes. These 
membranes are typically made up of nanomaterials that are 
spread throughout a matrix. Glass or rubber polymers can 
be utilized as an organic base matrix in the construction of 
nanocomposite membranes. Mineral nanoparticles can be 
used in the structure of nanocomposite membranes. Among 
the things are pure metals, metal oxides, zeolites (zeolite A4 
(Shameli et al. 2011), Silicate (Song et al. 2022), and ZSM-5 
(Al-Wasidi et al. 2022)), carbon (carbon nanotubes (Yazid 
et al. 2022), fullerene C60), etc. In the case of metal oxides, 
­SiO2 (Hamta et al. 2020), MgO (Azizi et al. 2023), AgO 
(Wang et al. 2022), ­Fe3O4 (Jahankhah et al. 2022), ­TiO2 
(Oliveira et al. 2022) and ­Al2O3 (Yousefi et al. 2023) have 
been already applied in different nanocomposite membranes.
Initially, these membranes were used to separation pro-
cess of gases, but more selective and permeable membranes 
were produced using zeolites (Choudhuri et al. 2207). 
Among the applications of these membranes, their use in 
sensors, fuel cells, water purification and evaporation can 
be mentioned (Hamta et al. 2017).

In particular, the use of these membranes for purifying 
oily wastewater can be attributed to research on sodium algi-
nate–graphene nanocomposite membranes for oil-in-water 
separation (Ehsan et al. 2023). In this paper, a hydrophilic 
nanocomposite membrane has been fabricated using GO 
nanosheets to produce an environmentally friendly, low-
cost, and sustainable membrane. The results show that the 
sodium alginate nanocomposite membranes are porous and 
hydrophilic membrane, which causes high purification per-
formance of the oil-in-water separation. The advancements 
in micro-machining techniques, such as those demonstrated 
by Li et al. (2023) using femtosecond lasers, offer insights 
into precise material modification. These principles could 
potentially be adapted for the controlled fabrication of nano-
composite membranes with tailored pore structures and 
functional properties.
Cellulose–polyethylene terephthalate nanofiber nano-
composite membrane made from waste materials has been 
applied for oil industry wastewater treatment (Bhuyan et al. 
2023). Oil industry wastewater contains many organic pol-
lutants, so the membranes used in this area must be resist-
ant to organic solvents. In this research, a super hydrophilic 
membrane has been introduced, which is prepared from 
recycled materials, namely polyethylene terephthalate, from 
plastic bottle caps and cellulose papers. The results show 
that the fabricated membranes have antibacterial properties 
in the presence of GO (Bhuyan et al. 2023).
In 2023, a polymer–ceramic nanocomposite membrane 
with high wettability was introduced for oily wastewater 
treatment (Baig and Waheed 2023). To fabricate the pol-
ymer–ceramic nanocomposite membrane, first, a layer of 
silicon dioxide is placed on silicon carbide, then it is func-
tionalized by an amino functional group and the composi-
tion is finally placed on an alumina support to fabricate the 
alumina supported NH2-SiO2@SiC as a membrane (Baig 
and Waheed 2023).
Recently, a super hydrophilic nanocomposite membrane 
modified with polydopamine-CaCO3 has been applied for 
treatment of oily wastewater. The ­CaCO3@PDA@nylon 
nanocomposite membrane was synthesized by dip-coating 
method utilizing dopamine and ­CaCO3 nanoparticle in 
Nylon 66 membrane in aqueous solution. The results show 
that the fabricated membranes have a good performance 
with high permeability and high anti-fouling properties 
(Shijie et al. 2022).
In 2022, Saejung et al. (2022) presented a magnetically 
recyclable biological nanocomposite for the oil droplets 
removal from water. Likewise, in 2023, a hydrogel-coated 
nanocomposite membrane has been prepared using one-step 
dip-coating method which shows that the hydrogel nano-
composite membranes can also be applied for separation 
of water and oil. The prepared nanocomposite was tannic 
acid/sodium alginate/3-aminopropyltriethoxysilane which 
has high hydrophilicity and electrophilic properties (Yan 
et al. 2023).
Although many studies have been conducted on oily 
wastewater treatment using composite membrane matrices, 
achieving an ideal separation process of oil in water emul-
sions with high performance requires new materials with 
superior properties to overcome the membrane anti-fouling 
bottleneck.
Graphene and its derivatives are one of the suitable 
options for various applications, such as the use in the syn-
thesis of various composites, due to its mechanical, chemi-
cal and electrical properties (Panahi-Sarmad et al. 2022). 
On the other hand, MXene is a new type of carbonitrides or 
transition metal carbides with a lamellar structure, which 
can produce the nanometer mass transfer channels (Hong 
et al. 2023).
In this work, silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) coated GO/
MXene nanocomposite membrane was prepared to optimize 
the efficiency of oily wastewater treatment. In this way, the 
obtained nanoparticles and fabricated membranes were char-
acterized properly. The anti-fouling and the antibacterial 
properties of the synthesized membranes were investigated 
by zeta potential analysis and the fouling mechanism was 
also correlated using Hermia fouling model. This study is 
expected to open a new way to prepare a high-performance 
membrane for treatment of oil contaminated wastewaters 
with anti-fouling and antibacterial properties.
Materials and methods
Polyamide 6 (PA6) was obtained from Sigma-Aldrich and 
was applied as the membrane matrix. Formic acid (Sigma-
Aldrich, ACS reagent, ≥ 98%), urea (Sigma-Aldrich, ACS 
reagent, 99%), and calcium chloride ­(CaCl2, Sigma-Aldrich, 
anhydrous powder, 99.99%) were applied for solvent prepa-
ration. The Titanium Carbide ­(Ti3C2T) MXene nanosheet 
was obtained from Laizhou Kai, China. In order to syn-
thesize the nanocomposite, polyvinylpyrrolidone powder 
with average molecular weight of ~ 55,000 g/mol, silver 
nitrate (ACS reagent, ≥ 99.0%), synthetic graphite pow-
der with average diameter of 20 μm, potassium persulfate 
­(K2S2O8, ACS reagent, ≥ 99.0%), sulfuric acid ­(H2SO4, 
99.99%), Potassium permanganate (ACS reagent, ≥ 99.0%), 
and Hydrogen peroxide 30% were purchased from Sigma-
Aldrich. Diesel oil was used for oil in water emulsion prepa-
ration and Tween80 was applied as emulsifier.
Silver nanoparticles‑coated GO synthesis
In order to synthesize the silver nanoparticles-Coated Gra-
phene oxide (SCG), first the silver NPs were synthesized

using heat treatment, and then Silver (II) oxide (AgO) nano-
particles were coated with synthesized GO.
To synthesize the silver nanoparticles (AgNPs), 7 g of 
polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP) was dissolved in 200 ml of 
ultrapure water (18.2 Mohm) at 90 °C using a magnetic stir-
rer. After the complete dissolution of the polymer, 0.5 mmol 
of silver nitrate ­(AgNO3) was slowly added to the obtained 
solution. The resulting solution was placed in the oven at 
100 °C for 24 h. Then, the dried material was gently milled 
for 130 min to obtain uniform fine powder. The resulting 
powder was placed in an oven at 650 °C for 4 h for calcina-
tion process and form the silver nanoparticles (Zein et al. 
2022).
The Hummers method has been applied in this work to 
prepare the GO (Zhu et al. 2022); briefly, 1 g of graphite 
along with 5 g potassium persulfate ­(K2S2O8) was mixed 
with water at a temperature of 70 °C using a stirrer to 
achieve a homogeneous solution. Then 25 ml of sulfuric 
acid was mixed to the prepared solution at 60 °C for 6 h. 
After that, the system received water that was exceptionally 
pure and was place for 12 h at ambient temperature; finally, 
the solution was filtered and dried properly. After drying, 
the resulting graphite oxide was poured into an Erlenmeyer 
flask and placed on a stirrer in a water bath at 10 °C, and 
200 ml of sulfuric acid solution and 30 g of potassium per-
manganate was applied in the solution and stirred for 5 min 
at 10 °C. Finally, 500 ml of ultrapure water and 150 ml of 
hydrogen peroxide was mixed to the solution and stirred for 
another 2 h at ambient temperature. In order to purify the 
synthesized GO and remove the metal ions, the product was 
centrifuged and washed using diluted ­H2SO4 (0.1 M) and 
was completely dried at 110 °C for 24 h.
After the silver nanoparticles and GO synthesis, these 
two synthesized materials were dissolved in ethanol as a 
solvent with an equal molar ratio of 1:1 for 24 h at 200 °C. 
The resulting sediment was separated and dried to be applied 
for further analysis and membrane fabrication.
Membrane preparation
To synthesize the membranes, first the desired solvent was 
synthesized by mixing formic acid with urea and calcium 
chloride. For this purpose, the materials were mixed with a 
weight ratio of 50 wt.% of formic acid, 20 wt.% of calcium 
chloride and 30 wt.% of urea for 60 min at ambient tempera-
ture using a magnetic stirrer. Then PA6 polymer was dis-
solved in the synthesized solvent and the desired amount of 
synthesized nanoparticles was added to the system (Waheed 
et al. 2022). The composition of the different synthesized 
membranes is presented in Table 1. It is worth noting that 
the fabricated membranes (Table 1) were also compared 
with the membranes containing silver nanoparticles or GO, 
which were labeled as MAg and MOG, respectively.
The dope solutions were prepared using a magnetic stir-
rer for 24 h at 40 °C and speed of 75 rpm. To synthesize 
the membranes, Non-solvent Induced Phase Separation 
(NIPS) method was used; in this way, the prepared dope 
solutions were casted using a casting machine on a glass 
plate and the solutions that were casted were promptly 
submerged into a coagulation bath containing water as the 
non-solvent (Hamta et al. 2020).
Oily wastewater preparation
To evaluate the fabricated membranes performances, a 
stable water/oil emulsion was synthesized as oily waste-
water. For this purpose, an emulsion of diesel oil with a 
concentration of 7500 mg/L was produced using Tween 80 
as a surfactant. In this way, the desired amounts of diesel 
oil, water and Tween 80 were mixed using a homogenizer 
for 20 min at 11,000 rpm. The size of oil particles in the 
produced wastewater was determined using DLS analysis 
(Alemu et al. 2022). As the results of the DLS analysis 
show in Fig. 1, the average size of the oil particles is equal 
to 1050 nm.
Membrane separation procedure
The membrane separation performance was investigated 
using a typical cross-flow membrane pilot system with a 
membrane module effective area of 30.2 ­cm2 and adjustable 
feed flow rate and effective pressure. The membrane separa-
tion pilot plant is illustrated in Fig. 2 schematically.
The efficacy of the membranes in treating oily wastewa-
ter can be computed using Eq. 1, where Cf and Cp repre-

Characterization
Characterization of the synthesized nanocomposite (SCG) 
was investigated by examining the diffraction patterns using 
X-ray Diffractometer (XRD, Malvern P analytical, UK) with 
a wavelength of λ = 1.50. To recognize the functional groups, 
Fourier Transform Infrared (FT-IR, Thermo Fisher Scientific, 
IS5, USA) analysis of the synthesized nanocomposite was per-
formed in the range of 400–4000 ­cm−1. The morphology of 
synthesized nanocomposite (SCG) was also evaluated using 
Ultra-High resolution analytical Field Emission Scanning 
Electron Microscopes (FE-SEM, SU7000, Hitachi, Japan). 
An Atomic Force Microscopes (AFM, NANBEI-1000, China) 
analysis was performed to study the three-dimensional mem-
brane sample surface with very high-resolution and to study 
the synthesized nanoparticles.
Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS, Otsuka, 8000DL/DH, 
Japan) was used to determine the size of oil particles in the 
synthesized wastewater. To calculate the swelling ratio of the 
obtained membranes Eq. 6 was used; where Ld and Lw are the

Results
Characterization
Figure 3 presents the FE-SEM images of GO (Fig. 3a) 
and SCG (Fig. 3b), which indicates the different surface 
morphology of GO with and without silver nanoparticles. 
Figure 3a exhibits a layered, sheet-like structure, char-
acterized by thick, stacked plates. This morphology is 
indicative of the aggregation of GO layers. Nevertheless, 
the wrinkled surface of the SCG nanocomposite in the 
scale of 1 µm presents in Fig. 3b. Comparing Fig. 3a with 
Fig. 3b, proves that the silver nanoparticles are uniformly 
dispersed on the GO surface, forming characteristic wrin-
kles and protrusions at the nanometer scale (Fatemi et al. 
2023).
The comparison of GO and SCG clearly demonstrates 
the successful incorporation of silver nanoparticles onto 
the GO surface. This modification has led to a substan-
tial change in the material's surface characteristics, which 
could have implications for its properties and performance 
in applications such as filtration and antibacterial activity.
The results of XRD analysis and the Raman spectra for 
synthesized GO and silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) sam-
ples are shown in Fig. 4. As shown in Fig. 4a, the sharp 
peaks of the XRD analysis show the synthesized nano-
composite crystalline nature (Alwan and Alshamsi 2022). 
In the interpretation of the X-ray diffraction patterns of 
the calcined samples, the cubic structure of silver nano-
particles with GO coating is confirmed. With the oxida-
tion of graphite and the addition of oxygenated functional 
groups to its structure, the distance between graphite 
layers increases and the peak related to graphite shifts to 
smaller angles; therefore, the position of the peak in terms 
of angle depends on the amount of graphite oxidation. 
Considering the observed peak for the synthesized GO 
in the range of 9.6°, it can be concluded that the graph-
ite is oxidized appropriately, and the GO is synthesized 
properly. According to Fig. 4b, D-band and G-band of the 
Raman spectra of the synthesized GO were observed in 
the range of 1600 ­cm−1 and 1380 ­cm−1 and for AgNPs in 
the range of 1548 ­cm−1 and 1290 ­cm−1 (Abaszade 2022). 
Characterizing the structure and properties of our nano-
composite membranes is essential for understanding their 
performance. Similar to the analysis conducted by Wellen-
dorf et al. (2023) on dynamic test benches, a rigorous test-
ing framework is needed to evaluate the structural integrity 
and functional properties of our membranes under various 
conditions (Wellendorf et al. 2023).
Figure 5 shows the FT-IR of the samples, which was 
carried out to identify the functional groups in the wave-
number range of 400–4000 ­cm−1. The GO peaks in the

range of 1840 ­cm−1 and 1480 ­cm−1 are related to the C = O 
functional group (Sudha et al. 2022). The peak of ­TiO2 
in the range of 700–900 ­cm−1 is evident in the MXene 
samples; Also, the 3321 ­cm−1 peak corresponds to O–H, 
which is characteristic of GO and confirms the presence 
of ­OH− and ­COOH− groups (Geng et al. 2022). The EDX 
analysis and the chemical compositions of the synthesized 
GO, AgNPs, and MXene are shown in Fig. 6.
The FTIR analysis primarily focused on character-
izing the GO and SCG materials. However, the absence 
of strong, characteristic peaks associated with specific 
functional groups on the silver nanoparticles suggests that 
they are likely coated with a thin layer of oxide or hydrox-
ide, which may have formed during the synthesis process.
The results of the analysis indicate that a smoother 
membrane surface is correlated with a higher FRR, sug-
gesting that a reduced surface roughness can improve 
the membrane's ability to recover its permeability after 
fouling. This observation aligns with previous studies 
(Hashino et al. 2011) that have highlighted the importance 
of surface morphology in determining membrane fouling 
behavior.

Conversely, we found that increasing the surface rough-
ness can reduce the water contact angle of the membranes. 
This is attributed to the increased surface area provided 
by the rougher surface, which can enhance the interac-
tion between the membrane and water molecules. A lower 
water contact angle generally indicates improved membrane 
hydrophilicity, which can be beneficial for reducing fouling 
and enhancing membrane performance (Woo et al. 2015).
In conclusion, our findings suggest that the surface mor-
phology of the fabricated membranes plays a crucial role 
in determining their fouling resistance and water contact 
angle. A smoother surface can contribute to improved FRR, 
while a rougher surface can lead to a reduced water contact 
angle. Future studies could explore strategies for tailoring 
the membrane surface morphology to optimize its perfor-
mance in specific applications.
The characteristics of different fabricated membranes 
are listed in Table 2. The results show that the hydrophilic 
membrane can be obtained using synthesized nanoparticles, 
which can increase the flux and improve the separation pro-
cess. As can be seen, the M2 membrane shows the lowest 
water contact angle as 33°, while the contact angle of the 
PA6 neat membrane (M0) is 83°.
The results indicate that the incorporation of synthe-
sized nanoparticles into the membrane matrix significantly 
enhances its hydrophilicity, as evidenced by the reduced 
water contact angle. This increased hydrophilicity can 
improve membrane performance by facilitating the wetting 
of the membrane surface and reducing the adhesion of fou-
lants (Yu et al. 2021).
The enhanced hydrophilicity of the nanoparticle-modi-
fied membranes can also lead to increased permeate flux, 
as water molecules can more readily pass through the mem-
brane pores. The hardness and Young's modulus of the mem-
branes provide insights into their mechanical strength and 
resistance to deformation. These properties are important 
for ensuring the long-term durability and stability of the 
membrane during operation.
To facilitate a more accurate comparison, the Hardness 
and Young’s modulus of different fabricated membranes are 
shown in Fig. 7. These results demonstrate that the introduc-
tion of nanoparticles can influence the mechanical properties 
of the membranes, potentially affecting their overall perfor-
mance and resistance to external stresses (Men et al. 2023).
Oily wastewater treatment
The performance of the M0, M2, M5, and M8 membranes 
was shown in Fig. 8 to investigate the SCG:MXene effect 
using 1 wt.% of nanoparticle. The permeate flux of the fab-
ricated membranes at the equilibrium condition (60 min) is 
depicted in Fig. 9.
The obtained data revealed that the rejection of all mem-
branes is above 99%, except PA6 neat membrane (M0), with 
the rejection of 97.9%, and MAg and MOG membranes, with 
the rejection of 98.3% and 98.5%, respectively (Fig. 10). 
Therefore, it can be concluded that more rejection has a 
direct relationship with the contact angle of the membranes. 
Figure 10 also shows that the M2 membrane contact angle 
has drastically decreased compared to M0. This reduction 
in contact angle is indicative of enhanced membrane hydro-
philicity, which can contribute to improved oil rejection and 
reduced fouling (Fan et al. 2018).

charge, is a critical parameter influencing the membrane's 
interaction with microorganisms and foulants.
As can be seen from Fig. 12, the M0 membrane is posi-
tive in all the pH ranges, consequently, it shows the high-
est biofouling properties. Nevertheless, the M2 membrane 
has shown the best performance in terms of antibacterial 
and anti-fouling, in view of the fact that the ζ/mV level 
has become negative at pH = 4. It can also be found that 
the MAg membrane performed better than M1 and MOG, 
which is due to the anti-fouling and antibacterial proper-
ties of silver nanoparticles, however its performance was 
worse than M2 (Kochkodan and Hilal 2015).
The M0 membrane consistently exhibited a positive 
zeta potential across the entire pH range. This positive 
surface charge can promote the adhesion of bacteria and 
other charged particles, leading to increased biofouling.
In contrast, the M2 membrane demonstrated a more 
favorable zeta potential profile, becoming negative at pH = 4. 
This negative surface charge can repel bacteria and other 
charged particles, reducing the likelihood of biofouling (Xu 
et al. 2020).
The MAg membrane exhibited intermediate antibacte-
rial and anti-fouling properties compared to M1 and MOG, 
likely due to the presence of silver nanoparticles. However, 
its performance was inferior to M2, suggesting that the com-
bination of GO, MXene, and silver nanoparticles in the M2 
membrane provides a more effective synergistic effect.

Membrane fouling analysis
Membrane fouling is the build-up of substances on or within 
the membrane matrix, resulting in the formation of cake lay-
ers on the membrane surface. These layers create additional 
resistance to fluid flow and as their thickness increases, the 
membrane resistance also increases correspondingly (Hamta 
et al. 2022).

To study the fouling mechanism of the synthesized mem-
branes, the classic Hermia fouling model was applied (Fan 
et al. 2018). In this model, Standard blocking mechanism, 
complete blocking mechanism, intermediate blocking and 
cake filtration mechanism are considered. The results of M1 
membrane fouling mechanisms are depicted in Fig. 15. The 
linear equations of Hermia fouling mechanism are listed in

The results of experimental data correlation on Hermia 
fouling model are shown in Table 4 in the form of R2 to 
investigate the model performance regression error. As can 
be seen from Table 4, the fouling mechanism of intermediate 
blocking has correlated the membrane fouling with better 
accuracy (Heidari et al. 2017).
Figure 16 shows the oily wastewater permeate flux using 
the M2 membrane as an example during the filtration pro-
cess in three cycles. As can be seen, the permeate water 
flux reduction can be related to the fouling of the internal 
membrane pores. Due to the accumulation of oily wastewa-
ter inside the pores, the flow channels are blocked; conse-
quently, the flux is decreased as expected.

Conclusions
This study presents the development of a novel nanocom-
posite membrane for the effective treatment of oily waste-
water. The membrane, fabricated using silver nanoparti-
cles (AgNPs) coated graphene oxide/MXene (GO/MXene) 
within a polyamide 6 (PA6) matrix, demonstrated excep-
tional performance in terms of oil rejection and fouling 
resistance. Key findings from this research include:
•	 Enhanced oil rejection: The nanocomposite membrane 
exhibited a high oil rejection rate of 99.0%, effectively 
removing oil contaminants from the wastewater.
•	 Superior anti-fouling properties: The modified mem-
branes demonstrated significantly improved anti-fouling 
properties compared to the pristine PA6 membrane. This 
is attributed to the synergistic effects of the GO, MXene, 
and AgNP components, which contribute to enhanced 
membrane hydrophilicity and reduced fouling propensity.

•	 High permeate flux: The nanocomposite membrane

•	 Effective fouling mitigation: The membrane fouling 
analysis showed that the modified membranes with 
FRR of 96.9% and Rt = 42.0% have higher sustainabil-
ity compared to the neat membrane with FRR of 65.6% 
and Rt = 89.7%. The fouling mechanism of the fabricated 
membranes was investigated using the classic Hermia 
fouling model, which revealed that intermediate block-
ing is the dominant fouling mechanism. This understand-
ing provides valuable insights for optimizing membrane 
design and operation.
Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of the 
developed nanocomposite membrane as a promising solu-
tion for the treatment of oily wastewater. The findings offer 
valuable insights for the development of industrial-scale 
membranes with enhanced performance and sustainabil-
ity. Future research could focus on further optimizing the 
membrane composition and exploring its application in real-
world wastewater treatment scenarios.

Abstract: There's growing interest in using membrane technology to treat oily wastewater in industries. Nevertheless, membrane foul- ing is still a major challenge for removing oil particles from the wastewater. As reducing the membrane fouling requires material and surface science insights, in this work, a nanocomposite membrane was investigated for oily wastewater treat- ment using synthesized silver nanoparticles (AgNPs) coated graphene oxide (GO)/MXene nanocomposite. The synthesized nanocomposite underwent characterization through FT-IR, XRD, FE-SEM, EDX, and Raman spectroscopy; and in order to characterize the fabricated membranes, SEM, and AFM analysis were applied and the membrane properties such as Hard- ness, Young’s modulus, thickness, swelling ratio, and Water Contact Angle were studied. The efficiency of the produced membranes was assessed by computing the membrane's oil rejection and permeate flow; the results showed that the rejec- tion was upper than 99.0% and the permeate flux was obtained as high as 160 L/m2 h. The study of the membrane surface charge by zeta potential analysis showed that the membrane performance could be optimized in terms of antibacterial and anti-fouling using synthesized nanocomposite membranes; that fully align with the findings of the efficiency of killing the bacteria (EKB) of different membranes using S. aureus as a Gram-positive and E. coli as a Gram-negative bacterium. The results of membrane fouling analysis showed that the modified membranes with FRR of 96.9% have higher sustainability compared to the PA6 neat membrane (FRR = 65.6%). Moreover, the classic Hermia fouling model revealed that the fouling mechanism of intermediate blocking best explains how fouling affects the membrane's performance.
